facts.statement: The genus Hesperornis was described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1872.
facts.quote: authority: Marsh, 1872

facts.statement: Fossils of Hesperornis date to the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, with possible records from the early Maastrichtian.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Cretaceous (Campanian), Possible early Maastrichtian record

facts.statement: Hesperornis was one of the lesser-known discoveries made by O. C. Marsh during the late 19th-century Bone Wars.
facts.quote: One of the lesser-known discoveries of the paleontologist O. C. Marsh in the late 19th century Bone Wars

facts.statement: Hesperornis fossils have been found in Late Cretaceous marine limestones in Kansas and marine shales in Canada.
facts.quote: Locations for Hesperornis fossils include the Late Cretaceous marine limestones from Kansas and the marine shales from Canada

facts.statement: Hesperornis was a large bird measuring between 1.5 and 2 meters in length and weighing approximately 10.6 kilograms.
facts.quote: Hesperornis was a large bird, measuring about 1.5 - 2 m long and weighing around 10.6 kg

facts.statement: Hesperornis had virtually no wings and swam using its powerful hind legs.
facts.quote: It had virtually no wings, and swam with its powerful hind legs

facts.statement: Like other Mesozoic birds such as Ichthyornis, Hesperornis possessed both teeth and a beak.
facts.quote: Like many other Mesozoic birds such as Ichthyornis, Hesperornis had teeth as well as a beak

facts.statement: The teeth of Hesperornis were located along nearly the entire lower jaw and the back of the upper jaw.
facts.quote: The teeth of Hesperornis were present along nearly the entire lower jaw (dentary) and the back of the upper jaw (maxilla)

facts.statement: The first Hesperornis specimen was discovered in 1871 by Othniel Charles Marsh.
facts.quote: The first Hesperornis specimen was discovered in 1871 by Othniel Charles Marsh

facts.statement: Marsh named the first specimen Hesperornis regalis, meaning "regal western bird".
facts.quote: Marsh named the find Hesperornis regalis, or "regal western bird"

facts.statement: Othniel Charles Marsh considered the initial Hesperornis specimen to be a diving species.
facts.quote: Marsh considered it a diving species

facts.statement: Thomas H. Russell, one of Marsh's students, discovered a nearly perfect skeleton of Hesperornis.
facts.quote: one of Marsh's four students, Thomas H. Russell, discovered a "nearly perfect skeleton" of Hesperornis

facts.statement: It is believed that a primitive joint in Hesperornis allowed the back portion of the lower jaw to rotate independently, enabling the teeth to disengage.
facts.quote: It is believed that this allowed them to rotate the back portion of the mandible independently of the front, thus allowing the lower teeth to disengage

facts.statement: Recent studies question whether Hesperornis had lobed or webbed toes, with both interpretations considered equally likely.
facts.quote: More recent work looking at the morphometrics of the feet in hesperornithiformes and modern sea birds has thrown this interpretation into question, making webbed toes equally as likely as lobed toes for this group

facts.statement: The best-known species, Hesperornis regalis, is known from dozens of specimens ranging from fragments to nearly complete skeletons found in the Smoky Hill Chalk Member of the Niobrara Formation.
facts.quote: H. regalis is also the best known species, and dozens of specimens (from fragments to more complete skeletons) have been recovered, all from the Smoky Hill Chalk Member of the Niobrara Formation

facts.statement: Othniel Charles Marsh named the smaller species Hesperornis gracilis in 1876 based on an incomplete metatarsus found in the same Niobrara chalk layers as H. regalis.
facts.quote: Marsh explicitly named his second species of Hesperornis in 1876 for an incomplete metatarsus recovered from the same layers of the Niobrara chalk as H. regalis. He named this smaller species H. gracilis

facts.statement: Hesperornis montana was named by Shufeldt in 1915 based on a single dorsal vertebra, which researchers consider distinct from H. altus due to its smaller size.
facts.quote: H. montana was named by Shufeldt in 1915, and while its known material (a single dorsal vertebra) cannot be directly compared to H. altus, Shufeldt and others have considered it distinct due to its apparently smaller size.

facts.statement: Nessov and Yarkov named Hesperornis rossicus in 1993 based on a fragmentary skeleton from the early Campanian of Russia near Volgograd, marking the first remains of the genus found outside North America.
facts.quote: In 1993, the first Hesperornis remains from outside of North America were recognized as a new species by Nessov and Yarkov. They named Hesperornis rossicus for a fragmentary skeleton from the early Campanian of Russia near Volgograd.

facts.statement: Hesperornis rossicus was about 1.4 meters long, making it the largest species of Hesperornis and one of the largest hesperornithines, though slightly smaller than the Canadian genus Canadaga.
facts.quote: At about 1.4 m long, H. rossicus was the largest species of Hesperornis and among the largest hesperornithines, slightly smaller than the large Canadian genus Canadaga.

facts.statement: Hesperornis is a genus of marine birds that lived during the Late Cretaceous, between the Santonian and Campanian stages, approximately 89 to 78 million years ago.
facts.quote: Hesperornis (gr. Ave del oeste) es un género de aves marinas que vivieron en el Cretácico superior, entre el Santoniense y el Campaniense, hace unos 89-78 millones de años.

facts.statement: Hesperornis lived in North America from Kansas to Canada within an inland sea, as well as in the waters of the Turgai Strait near Siberia.
facts.quote: Vivió en Norteamérica, desde Kansas hasta Canadá, en un mar interior que cubría parte de Norteamérica, y también en las aguas del estrecho de Turgai, cerca de Siberia.

facts.statement: Hesperornis was primarily marine, inhabiting subtropical to tropical shallow seas like the Western Interior Seaway, the Turgai Strait, and the North Sea.
facts.quote: Hesperornis was primarily marine, and lived in the waters of such contemporary shallow shelf seas as the Western Interior Seaway, the Turgai Strait, and the North Sea, which then were subtropical to tropical waters, much warmer than today.

facts.statement: Youngest specimens found in the freshwater Foremost Formation suggest that some Hesperornis species may have partially abandoned their primarily marine habitat for inland waters.
facts.quote: However, some of the youngest known specimens of Hesperornis have been found in inland freshwater deposits of the Foremost Formation, suggesting that some species of Hesperornis may have eventually moved, at least partially, away from a primarily marine habitat.

facts.statement: Studies of limb proportions and hip structure confirm that Hesperornis moved in a manner similar to modern loons or grebes.
facts.quote: Traditionally, Hesperornis is depicted with a mode of locomotion similar to modern loons or grebes, and study of their limb proportions and hip structure has borne out this comparison.

facts.statement: Hesperornis were likely excellent foot-propelled divers but probably moved ungainly on land.
facts.quote: Like loons, Hesperornis were probably excellent foot-propelled divers, but might have been ungainly on land.

facts.statement: Hesperornis legs were likely encased in the body wall up to the ankle, preventing them from standing or walking normally; instead, they probably moved on land by belly-sliding like modern seals.
facts.quote: Like loons, the legs were probably encased inside the body wall up to the ankle, causing the feet to jut out to the sides near the tail. This would have prevented them from bringing the legs underneath the body to stand, or under the center of gravity to walk. Instead, they likely moved on land by pushing themselves along on their bellies, like modern seals.

facts.statement: The genus Hesperornis was established by Marsh in 1872.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Marsh, 1872

facts.statement: Species within the genus include H. regalis (type species, 1872), H. crassipes (1876), H. gracilis (1876), H. altus (1893), H. montana (1915), H. rossicus (1993), and several species described by Martin and Lim in 2002.
facts.quote: subdivision: H. regalis Marsh, 1872 (especie tipo) H. crassipes (Marsh, 1876) [originalmente Lestornis] H. gracilis Marsh, 1876 H. altus (Marsh, 1893) [originalmente Coniornis] H. montana Schufeldt, 1915 H. rossicus Nesov & Yarkov, 1993 H. bairdi Martin & Lim, 2002 H. chowi Martin & Lim, 2002 H. macdonaldi Martin & Lim, 2002 H. mengeli Martin & Lim, 2002

facts.statement: Hesperornis was a large bird reaching up to 1.8 meters in length.
facts.quote: Eran aves de gran tamaño, de hasta 1,8 metros de longitud.

facts.statement: Hesperornis had a near-total absence of wings due to highly reduced forelimbs.
facts.quote: Se caracterizaban por la práctica ausencia de alas (los miembros anteriores estaban muy reducidos)

facts.statement: Hesperornis possessed lobed feet similar to those of grebes.
facts.quote: unas patas con pies lobulados (semejantes a los de los somormujos)

facts.statement: Hesperornis was a non-flying bird that lived primarily in water.
facts.quote: Hesperornis era por tanto un ave no voladora y principalmente acuática.

facts.statement: Hesperornis could not walk because its feet were positioned to the sides of its body, forcing it to drag itself like a seal.
facts.quote: los pies del Hesperornis no podían situarse bajo su cuerpo, y por lo tanto no podía caminar, teniendo que moverse arrastrando el cuerpo tal y como hacen las focas.

facts.statement: Hesperornis used teeth to hold onto prey, which were likely fish.
facts.quote: Hesperornis tenía dientes que utilizaba para sostener a sus presas (probablemente peces).

facts.statement: Hesperornis featured a unique arrangement of teeth in a longitudinal jaw rather than individual sockets, showing convergent evolution with mosasaurs.
facts.quote: con los dientes situados en una mandíbula longitudinal en vez de en espacios individuales, en un caso notable de evolución convergente con mosasaurios.

facts.statement: Hesperornis had teeth on the lower jaw and rear upper jaw, while toothless areas were covered by a keratinous beak.
facts.quote: Los dientes se distribuían por la mandíbula inferior y la parte trasera de la superior, mientras que en las zonas con ausencia de dientes (parte de la mandíbula superior y la punta de la inferior) estarían cubiertas por un pico queratinoso

facts.statement: Marsh named the initial discovery Hesperornis regalis, meaning "royal western bird".
facts.quote: Marsh nombró al hallazgo Hesperornis regalis, es decir "ave occidental real".

facts.statement: Thomas H. Russell, one of Marsh's students, discovered an "almost perfect" Hesperornis skeleton.
facts.quote: uno de los cuatro estudiantes de Marsh, Thomas H. Russell, descubrió un «esqueleto casi perfecto» de Hesperornis.

facts.statement: Marsh recognized the important evolutionary implications of finding Hesperornis alongside Benjamin Mudge's discovery of another toothed bird, Ichthyornis.
facts.quote: Marsh vio las importantes implicaciones evolutivas de su hallazgo, junto con el descubrimiento de Benjamin Mudge de otra ave dentada, Ichthyornis.

facts.statement: In a 1873 article, Marsh stated that finding these fossils helped dismantle the old distinction between birds and reptiles.
facts.quote: En un artículo de 1873 Marsh declaró que «el afortunado hallazgo de estos interesantes fósiles ha hecho mucho por echar abajo la antigua distinción entre Aves y Reptiles».

facts.statement: Marsh eventually received parts from 50 Hesperornis specimens, allowing him to provide a much stronger demonstration of the evolutionary link between birds and reptiles.
facts.quote: Acabaría recibiendo partes de 50 especímenes de Hesperornis, lo que le permitió hacer una demostración mucho más fuerte del vínculo evolutivo entre aves y reptiles de lo que antes había sido posible.

facts.statement: Hesperornis fossils were first found in Kansas during Marsh's second expedition to the West.
facts.quote: El primer espécimen de Hesperornis fue descubierto en 1871 por Othniel Charles Marsh.

facts.statement: The initial specimen found by Marsh was a large fossil bird at least five feet tall.
facts.quote: Marsh descubrió el esqueleto de una «gran ave fósil, de al menos cinco pies de altura».

facts.statement: Hesperornis belongs to the family Hesperornithidae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Hesperornithidae

facts.statement: Hesperornis is classified within the class Reptilia.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: Hesperornis lived from the Coniacian to the Maastrichtian, between 89.8 and 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Coniacian to Maastrichtian (89.8 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: The first species described in the genus was the type species Hesperornis regalis.

facts.statement: Hesperornis regalis is the best-known species, with dozens of specimens recovered.
facts.quote: H. regalis es también la especie mejor conocida, y se han recuperado docenas de especímenes

facts.statement: Hesperornis regalis is the only species of Hesperornis known from a complete skull.
facts.quote: Es la única especie de Hesperornis de la cual se conoce un cráneo completo.

facts.statement: Hesperornis crassipes was larger than H. regalis and had five ribs instead of four.
facts.quote: H. crassipes era mayor que H. regalis, tenía cinco costillas a diferencia de las cuatro de la primera especie

facts.statement: Marsh explicitly named his second Hesperornis species in 1876 based on an incomplete metatarsal.
facts.quote: Marsh nombró explícitamente a su segunda especies de Hesperornis en 1876 de un metatarso incompleto

facts.statement: Hesperornis altus lived 78 million years ago in Montana.

facts.statement: In 1993, Nessov and Yarkov recognized the first Hesperornis fossils found outside North America as a new species.
facts.quote: En 1993, los primeros restos de Hesperornis conocidos por fuera de Norteamérica fueron reconocidos como una nueva especie por Nessov y Yarkov.

facts.statement: Hesperornis rossicus was about 1.4 meters long and was the largest species of Hesperornis.
facts.quote: Con cerca de 1.4 metros de largo, H. rossicus fue la mayor especie de Hesperornis

facts.statement: In 2002, Martin and Lim formally recognized several new species of Hesperornis.
facts.quote: En 2002, Martin y Lim reconocieron formalmente a varias nuevas especies

facts.statement: The species recognized by Martin and Lim included the small H. mengeli and H. macdonaldi, the slightly larger H. bairdi, and the enormous H. chowi.
facts.quote: Estas especies incluyen a los pequeños H. mengeli y H. macdonaldi, el levemente mayor H. bairdi, y al enorme H. chowi

facts.statement: Hesperornis was primarily a marine bird that lived in epicontinental seas.

facts.statement: The diet of Hesperornis consisted mainly of fish and other aquatic creatures.
facts.quote: La dieta de Hesperornis se componía principalmente de peces y otras criaturas acuáticas.

facts.statement: Young specimens of Hesperornis grew rapidly and continuously, like modern birds.
facts.quote: Los ejemplares jóvenes de estas aves crecían rápidamente y a un ritmo continuo, como las aves modernas.

facts.statement: Hesperornis was one of the first prehistoric birds identified.
facts.quote: Hesperornis fue una de las primeras aves prehistóricas identificadas

facts.statement: Hesperornis appeared in the TV fiction series Primeval and the BBC documentary series Sea Monsters.
